mercy_translation.text:
That death has been destroyed, that the cross has become a victory over it, and that it no longer possesses strength but is truly dead—of this there is no small sign and clear proof: all Christ's disciples despise death. They trample upon it, no longer fear it, and by the sign of the cross and faith in Christ tread it down as something dead.

Before the divine coming of the Savior, death was fearful even to the saints, and all mourned those who died as though they were being destroyed. But now that the Savior has raised the body, death is no longer terrible. All who believe in Christ tread upon it as though it were nothing, and choose to die rather than deny their faith in Christ. For they truly know that when they die they do not perish, but live and through the resurrection become incorruptible.

But that devil who once leaped wickedly in death, now that death's birth-pangs have been loosed, remains himself truly dead. Proof of this is that before people believe in Christ they regard death as terrible and are afraid of it; but when they pass over into his faith and teaching, they so despise death that they willingly rush toward it and become witnesses to the resurrection accomplished by the Savior against it.

Even those young in age hasten toward death, and not only men but women train themselves against it through ascetic exercises. So weak has death become that even women who were once deceived by it now mock it as dead and powerless.

It is like a tyrant who, having been defeated by a true king and bound hand and foot, is thereafter mocked by everyone passing by: they strike him and insult him, no longer fearing his rage or savagery because of the victorious king. So too, since death has been conquered and exposed by the Savior on the cross and bound hand and foot, all who pass over into Christ trample it down. Bearing witness to Christ, they mock death and taunt it with the words written against it long ago: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O Hades, is your sting?”

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius uses the courage of martyrs and ascetics as experiential evidence that Christ has broken death's power.
The tyrant analogy portrays death as publicly defeated and stripped of its former terror.
